content.text: prawns, enough to serve 4 as a starter, and takes about 35 minutes. The prawns are coated in a barely-mixed batter and fried at a precise temperature to give a crust that is crisp and almost transparent. They are served with
, a warm dipping sauce built on

The batter must be cold and lumpy. This is the opposite of everything you know about batters. Cold batter hits the hot oil and creates steam instantly, which makes the crust light and airy. Lumps of unmixed flour in the batter become crisp frills as they fry. Use ice water. Mix with chopsticks in fewer than 10 strokes. Do not use a whisk. Do not overmix. The batter should look like thin, barely-combined cream with streaks of dry flour still visible.

Prepare the prawns. Peel them, leaving the tail on. Devein by running a small knife along the back and removing the dark thread. Make 3 shallow cuts across the belly of each prawn and press gently to straighten. This stops them curling up in the oil.

Make the tentsuyu. Combine the dashi, soy sauce and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 2 minutes. Remove from the heat. Keep warm. Set the grated ginger in a small dish alongside.

Pour the vegetable oil into a wok to a depth of about 5cm. Heat over a medium-high heat to 175 to 180 degrees C. Use a thermometer. If you do not have one, drop a tiny pinch of batter in: it should sink slightly, then float and sizzle immediately.

Make the batter just before frying. Whisk the egg yolk with 150ml of ice-cold water. Add the cornflour all at once. Stir with chopsticks in under 10 strokes. The batter will look thin and lumpy. This is correct. Do not mix further.
Hold each prawn by the tail and dip it into the batter. Let the excess drip off for a second. Lower it into the oil. Fry 3 to 4 prawns at a time. Do not overcrowd the wok.

Fry for 2 to 2.5 minutes until the batter is pale gold and the prawn is cooked through. The batter should be almost white with a very light colour, not deeply browned. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack over kitchen paper.
Serve immediately on warmed plates with small bowls of tentsuyu for dipping. Add a pinch of grated ginger to the tentsuyu before dipping each prawn.

items.symptom: The batter is heavy and doughy rather than crisp
items.cause: Batter was overmixed or the water was not cold enough
items.fix: Use water with ice cubes in it. Mix the batter for no more than 10 strokes with chopsticks. Lumps are good. Make the batter fresh for each batch if frying in multiple rounds.

items.symptom: The batter slips off the prawn in the oil
items.cause: The prawn was too wet before dipping
items.fix: Pat the prawns completely dry with kitchen paper before dipping in batter. Any surface moisture will prevent the batter sticking.

items.symptom: The oil temperature drops between batches and the batter absorbs oil
items.cause: Too many prawns added at once or not enough oil
items.fix: Fry no more than 3 to 4 prawns at a time. Let the oil return to temperature between batches. Adding cold prawns drops the temperature, and a cool oil produces a greasy, soft crust.

content.text: Tempura was introduced to Japan by Portuguese missionaries in the 16th century. Japanese cooks made the batter much lighter. It became a street food in Edo, sold at stalls. Today it appears at home, in specialist restaurants, and as a topping on noodle dishes.
